intro: Seven mats that keep snowmelt, road salt and oil off your concrete, from full-car containment mats to drip pads. The AutoFloorGuard AFG7918 is the pick for most snowy-climate garages.

A garage floor mat is the cheapest way to protect concrete, and the most misunderstood. A containment mat, a roll-out vinyl floor and an absorbent drip pad solve three different problems, and buying the wrong one means a puddle of salty slush spreading under your workbench or a slick sheet of vinyl that does nothing for the oil leak. This guide sorts seven real mats by the job they do, so you can match the mat to what is actually landing on your floor.
quickAnswer: the AutoFloorGuard AFG7918 Mid-Size Garage Containment Mat is our #1 pick (best overall / best for snow). The containment mat to buy if winter slush is your main enemy and you drive a car or small SUV.

THE RULE
Match the mat to the liquid.
Water and snowmelt need containment: a raised edge. Oil needs absorption: a pad with a waterproof backing. Stains and ugly concrete need coverage: roll-out vinyl. One mat rarely does all three well.

sections.h: The Three Kinds of Garage Floor Mat

blocks.p: **Containment mats** are flexible PVC sheets with a raised perimeter, usually a foam or rolled edge around an inch high. They are built for one job: holding the snow, slush and salt brine that drips off a car after a winter drive. Without one, that water spreads across the floor, carries road salt into every crack and expansion joint, and refreezes into ice near the door. With one, it sits in a tray until it evaporates or you push it out with a squeegee.

**Roll-out vinyl flooring**, like G-Floor's ribbed and coin-pattern rolls, is a floor covering rather than a tray. It is thicker, stiffer and nicer looking, and it hides stains, cracks and spalling. It sheds water toward the door through its texture, but it does not contain it. It is the choice for a garage that doubles as a workshop or a gym, or simply for someone who wants the floor to look finished without the prep work and fumes of a coating.

**Absorbent mats and drip pads** use a fibrous top over a waterproof backing. They come in two scales: car-length parking mats like the Armor All Original and the G-Floor Drip and Dry, and small pads like the Armor All and Drymate oil spill mats that sit under an engine. They soak up drips rather than letting them stand, which makes them less slippery and better for oil, but they cannot hold a winter's worth of meltwater.

Plenty of garages benefit from two kinds at once. A common and effective setup in snow country is a containment mat for winter, rolled away in spring, with a drip pad left under the engine year round. On an epoxy-coated or tiled floor, a drip pad alone is often enough, because the coating already shrugs off water and salt.

Capacity is listed only where the maker or a retailer publishes it; most containment mat makers do not publish a figure for every size, and those that do measure it in ideal conditions on a perfectly flat floor, which no garage has.

Size is the second deciding column. Measure your vehicle's length and width, add at least a foot on each side for drips from doors and bumpers, and compare that to the mat. A containment mat that is a little too short is worse than useless in heavy snow, because the overflow goes straight onto bare concrete at the front or back where you least expect it.

The drip pads are cheap enough that most garages should own one regardless of what else they buy. They cost little, they protect the most expensive mess to clean, and they let you spot a new leak by its color before it becomes a problem.

sections.h: What to Look For in a Garage Floor Mat

blocks.p: On a containment mat, the edge is the product. Look for a continuous raised edge that will not flatten permanently when you drive over it. Foam-filled edges recover their shape well; folded or rolled edges can crease. Edges around an inch high are typical. Higher sounds better but makes the mat harder to drive onto and more likely to snag a low front spoiler or a snow blower.

Containment mats are usually coated PVC fabric; roll-out flooring is solid polyvinyl measured in mils, where 55 mil is a standard grade and 75 mil and up is heavier commercial grade. Thicker vinyl lies flatter and resists tire marks better. For absorbent mats, what matters most is the backing: a bonded waterproof layer is what keeps oil from reaching the concrete, and a mat without one is just a rug.

Measure the vehicle and the space before you shop. Most mats are sized by vehicle class rather than exact dimensions, and two brands' mid-size can differ by a couple of feet. Leave room to walk around the mat, and keep it clear of floor drains, which should stay uncovered so you can sweep water into them.

A wet sheet of smooth PVC is slippery. Look for a textured or ribbed surface on roll-out flooring, and remember that absorbent mats are the least slippery option when wet. On a containment mat, the safest habit is to step out of the car onto dry concrete at the side rather than into the tray.

Road salt, oil and antifreeze are what garage mats live with. PVC containment mats handle salt brine well. Some vinyls stain from hot tires or certain oils; check the maker's guidance on hot-tire pickup if you drive in from a long highway run. Absorbent mats will stain; that is how they work, and you replace them when they are saturated.

sections.h: Sizing a Mat to Your Vehicle

blocks.p: Start with the vehicle's overall length and width at the mirrors, which you can find in the owner's manual or the manufacturer's spec page. A typical midsize sedan is about 16 feet long and just over 6 feet wide without mirrors; a crew-cab full-size pickup can be 19 to 20 feet long and more than 6.5 feet wide. Add about 12 inches in front and behind, and 6 to 12 inches on each side, and that is the minimum footprint a containment mat should cover.

That math is why the AFG7918's 18-foot length suits sedans, crossovers and small SUVs, while full-size trucks need the AFG8520's 20 feet. It is also why a 17-foot absorbent mat like the Armor All Original works for most cars but leaves the tailgate drips of a pickup on bare concrete. If you are between sizes, go bigger; a few extra inches of mat cost nothing in use, and too little mat costs you a puddle.

Next, check the garage. Measure from the door threshold to the back wall and from the side wall to the next vehicle or the workbench. A containment mat should lie flat across its whole area, so do not let it ride up against a wall, a step or a shelf leg. If the floor slopes toward the door, as most do, position the mat so its front edge sits a few inches inside the threshold, which keeps the low end of the tray inside the garage.

For drip pads, measure where the leak actually lands. Park, let the car sit overnight on a sheet of cardboard, and look in the morning. Engine oil usually lands under the front third of the car; transmission and rear-axle leaks further back. Place the pad there, not in the center of the bay where it looks tidy.

sections.h: Mats vs Epoxy, Coatings and Tiles

blocks.p: A mat protects concrete; a coating or tile floor changes it. Epoxy and polyaspartic coatings seal the surface so water, salt and oil sit on top instead of soaking in, and a well-done coating is easier to clean than any mat. If you plan to keep the house for years, a coating is the better long-term investment, and our [garage floor epoxy guide](/best-garage-floor-epoxy/) walks through which kits are worth the prep work.

Coatings have limits, though. Even a good epoxy floor can be slick when wet, and winter salt brine left standing on it for months still dulls the finish over time. That is why many owners with coated floors still lay a containment mat in winter: the coating protects the concrete, and the mat keeps the brine in one place where it can be pushed out the door.

Interlocking tiles are the third option. They hide damaged concrete, let water drain underneath through vented designs, and can be pulled up and moved. Our guide to the [best garage floor tiles](/best-garage-floor-tiles/) covers the main systems. Tiles cost more than roll-out vinyl and less than a professional coating, and they are the best choice for a floor that is too cracked or damp to coat reliably.

If your floor already has oil stains, deal with them before you lay any mat or coating; a mat over an active stain just hides it, and a coating will not bond to oily concrete. Our guide on [how to get oil out of concrete](/how-to-get-oil-out-of-concrete/) covers the poultice and degreaser methods that actually lift old stains, and it is worth an afternoon before you roll out new flooring.

Containment mats need the most attention. In heavy snow, push the water out of the tray every few days with a floor squeegee rather than letting it reach the edge. The salt stays behind as a white crust when the water evaporates; sweep it up, or hose the mat down on a mild day and squeegee it out the door. Letting brine sit all winter is what makes the mat smell and stains the PVC.

In spring, roll the containment mat out onto the driveway, wash both sides with a mild detergent and a soft brush, rinse, and let it dry completely before rolling it for storage. Store it rolled, not folded, so the edges do not take a permanent crease. A clean, dry mat stored this way will last many winters.

Roll-out vinyl can be mopped, scrubbed or pressure washed. Clean up oil spills promptly, because some oils will stain vinyl if they sit, and use a vinyl-safe degreaser rather than solvents. If a hot tire leaves a mark, a little dish soap and a nylon brush usually lifts it. Absorbent mats can be vacuumed, and the Drymate and Armor All drip pads can be scrubbed with soap, hosed off and hung to dry; do not use bleach on them.

Finally, check underneath any mat once or twice a season. Moisture can collect under a mat on a floor with a high water table, and a hidden leak can soak through a worn backing. Lift a corner, look, and dry the concrete if needed. It takes a minute and catches problems before they stain the slab.

sections.h: Which Garage Floor Mat Should You Buy?

blocks.p: **Snow country, car or small SUV:** the AutoFloorGuard AFG7918. A raised-edge containment mat is the only kind of mat that genuinely holds winter meltwater, and this one fits most vehicles that are not full-size trucks.
**Snow country, truck or full-size SUV:** the AutoFloorGuard AFG8520. It is long and wide enough to catch the drips from bumpers, doors and tailgate, with a listed capacity of up to 64 gallons.

**Ugly or stained floor, mild winters:** the G-Floor Ribbed Parking Pad. It makes the garage look finished in an hour, sheds water toward the door and needs no curing time. If you want something that absorbs rather than sheds, the G-Floor Drip and Dry is the absorbent alternative.

**Tight budget:** the Armor All Original Garage Floor Mat covers a full car length for less than any containment mat and soaks up wet tire tracks and light drips. Do not expect it to hold heavy snowmelt.

**Oil leak:** the Armor All Premium Oil Spill Mat under the engine, or the Drymate 29 x 36 under a bike or mower. Every garage should have one. And if you are thinking about a permanent upgrade, compare the cost of mats over a few winters against the coatings in our [epoxy roundup](/best-garage-floor-epoxy/) before you decide.

mistakes: Buying an absorbent mat for heavy snow

Absorbent parking mats look substantial, but they have no edge and a limited capacity. A car that brings in a few inches of packed snow will saturate the top layer within days, and the overflow runs onto the concrete. If you get real winters, buy a containment mat with a raised edge and keep the absorbent mat for the rest of the year.
Buying a mat that is too short

A containment mat that stops at the bumpers leaves the heaviest drips, from the wheel wells and the front fascia, landing on bare concrete. Measure the vehicle, add about a foot at each end, and buy the size that covers it. When in doubt between two sizes, go bigger; extra coverage never causes a problem.

Many garages have a floor drain near the center or the door. Laying a mat over it traps water underneath and stops you squeegeeing meltwater into the drain. Position the mat so the drain stays exposed, or trim roll-out vinyl around it with a utility knife and a straightedge.
Laying a mat over an oil-soaked slab

A mat over an active oil stain hides the problem but does not stop it spreading, and trapped oil can soften some vinyls over time. Clean the stain first with a degreaser or poultice, let the concrete dry, then lay the mat. For coatings, oily concrete is a guaranteed bond failure.

A containment mat holds water; it does not make it disappear. Leaving brine standing all winter lets salt crust build up, creates a smell and risks overflow during a big storm. Push the water out with a squeegee every few days in heavy snow, and rinse the mat on the first mild day.
bottomLine: The best garage floor mat is the one that matches what lands on your floor. For winter slush, that means a containment mat with a raised edge, and the AutoFloorGuard AFG7918 is the one to buy for most cars. For oil, it means an absorbent drip pad with a waterproof backing under the engine. Roll-out vinyl and absorbent parking mats fill the gaps in between: a better-looking floor, wet tire tracks, light drips. Buy for the job, size it to the vehicle, empty it in winter, and your concrete will look the same in ten years as it does today.

faqs.q: What is the best garage floor mat for snow?
faqs.a: A containment mat with a raised edge is the best garage floor mat for snow, because it holds meltwater and road salt in a tray instead of letting it spread. The AutoFloorGuard AFG7918 suits most cars and small SUVs, and the larger AFG8520 suits full-size trucks. Absorbent mats cannot hold a winter's worth of snowmelt.

faqs.q: Do garage containment mats really work?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as you size them correctly and empty them. A containment mat keeps salty meltwater off the concrete and in one place, where you can squeegee it out the door. Problems come from mats that are too short for the vehicle, or from owners who let water sit until it overflows the edge.

faqs.q: What do you put under a car to catch oil?
faqs.a: Use an absorbent oil drip mat with a waterproof backing, such as the 30 by 59 inch Armor All Premium Oil Spill Mat. It soaks up oil, coolant and brake fluid and stops them reaching the concrete. Place it where the drip actually lands, usually under the front third of the car, and fix the leak as soon as you can.

faqs.q: Are roll-out vinyl garage floor mats worth it?
faqs.a: Roll-out vinyl, such as G-Floor, is worth it if you want the floor to look finished without the prep and curing time of a coating. It hides stains and cracks and is easy to clean. It does not contain water, so in snowy climates pair it with a containment mat in winter, or choose a coating or tiles instead.

faqs.q: How do you keep a garage floor mat from moving?
faqs.a: Containment mats are heavy enough to stay put once flattened. Roll-out vinyl and absorbent mats can creep under hot tires, so tape the leading edge and corners with double-sided carpet tape, which some mats include. Let a new vinyl mat relax in a warm garage for a day before taping so it lies completely flat.

faqs.q: Can you put a garage mat on an epoxy floor?
faqs.a: Yes. Containment mats and drip pads are safe on cured epoxy and are a common winter addition, since standing brine can dull even a good coating. Wait until the coating is fully cured per the maker's instructions, usually several days, and avoid rubber-backed mats on fresh coatings, which can occasionally discolor them.

faqs.q: How do you clean a garage containment mat?
faqs.a: Push standing water out with a floor squeegee, sweep up salt residue, then on a mild day roll the mat onto the driveway and wash it with mild detergent and a soft brush. Rinse, let both sides dry completely, and store it rolled rather than folded so the containment edge does not crease.
